They leave players alone, but a player who hurts a villager or a golem of a village is its enemy for 5 minutes, and a golem that is hurt is angry with the player for 30 seconds; golems you built never attack players. Repair a hurt golem by using an iron ingot on it. A golem drops iron ingots and sometimes poppies.
sections.title: Building and keeping golems

sections.text: Villagers open wooden doors on their way and close them behind them; iron doors stay shut for them. A long way through the village, say across the boardwalks of a swamp village, goes along the roads in stages, so villagers find their way home from every corner of their village.
sections.title: Doors and long ways

sections.text: A creature kind lives in villages with `"villager": "<settings>"`, naming its species' file in `villagers/`: the daily routine as steps through the day (wander, work, meet, home, sleep), how far it flees, trading, `breeding` (the food a parent needs, how farmers share, how long children take to grow up and parents rest) and the default look. Each profession is its own file in `professions/`: the blocks it works at, layers laid over the outfit, a hat, whether it tends crops, and optionally its own routine; two mods each adding a profession keep both. A village style dresses its villagers with `look` in its file (an outfit, hair styles and hats to choose from and lists of skin, hair, shirt and trouser colours), may name its own villager kind and golems and lists other residents. `worldgen/villages.json` names the villagers and the golem of all other villages and its thresholds.
sections.title: Villagers in mods

sections.text: Villages stand on flat land in plains, deserts, taiga and tundra, and on stilts in the wet parts of swamps; never in oceans, mountains or forests. The world is divided into square regions (384 blocks in the base game), and a region holds at most one village, about half a region away from the next. Where a village goes depends only on the seed, so a world of the same seed has its villages in the same places. Operators find the nearest one with `/locate village`; `/village` shows its state.
sections.title: Finding villages

sections.text: Each biome builds in its own style. Plains villages are made of oak and cobblestone with pitched roofs of stairs, a well with a bell in the middle, main roads of cobblestone or gravel, side roads of dirt path and lamp posts. Desert villages are made of sandstone and terracotta with flat roofs, main roads of terracotta or packed mud that stand out against the sand, side roads of cut sandstone and fields with sugar cane by the water. Taiga villages are the plains houses in spruce. Snowy villages in the tundra mix igloos of snow blocks with ice windows, spruce cabins under a layer of snow and the larger plains houses in spruce, with main roads of packed ice or gravel. Swamp villages stand in the water on stilts of dark spruce: huts with thatched roofs, a meeting hall with the bell on a large platform in the middle, a fisher's hut, a herb hut with mushrooms and raised fields, all joined by boardwalks at one height above the water, with stairs down where a boardwalk reaches dry land. Around them the swamp is marshland: irregular pools of shallow water ringed by mud, grass between them and sugar cane at the water. A biome that has villages but no style of its own (one a mod adds) builds in the plains style.
sections.title: Styles

sections.text: Every village has its own street plan: one long main street through the middle with side streets, four roads from the well to all sides, three in a T or two in an L, a ring road around a square with the well, or roads at all angles that bend; some roads wind along the slopes. Diagonal roads run as staircases, and the houses at them have a forecourt to the road. Roads stop at water and steep slopes. Along them stand small and large houses with beds, fields of wheat, carrots and potatoes, ripe and still growing, with water and paths between the rows, a smithy with furnaces and a church or temple, each with its door to the road. Every kind of house comes in several designs, and no two houses need to look alike: walls of oak, birch or spruce, roofs of wood, cobblestone or brick, a chimney, flowers in front, a shed beside, terracotta in different colours in the desert. Some villages have an animal pen with a pair of pigs or sheep; a village near water has a fisher's hut with a jetty out over the water; large villages have a stone watchtower, taller than every house, with a ladder up to its battlements. Where a main road climbs a terrace by one block, a slab makes the step. Lanterns light the houses inside and lamp posts the roads, so no monsters spawn in them. Houses rest on a foundation where the ground is uneven, and the ground above them is cleared.
sections.title: Buildings

sections.text: The world remembers every village: its middle, its area, its beds and its workstations (composter: farmer, furnace: smith, barrel: fisher). Beds and workstations you place or break inside a village count at once; one placed up to 32 blocks from a village's buildings joins it, and the area grows, but never into another village's: every bed and workstation belongs to one village. A bed or workstation farther from every village starts a settlement of its own: villagers without a home move in, and it lives like any village (children, golems). A settlement without beds, workstations and villagers is forgotten. Villagers claim a bed and a workstation each (see Villagers). A village lists at most 64 beds and 64 workstations (one placed beyond that is not listed later either); the server limits `villageBeds`, `villageWorkstations` and `villages` change that.
sections.title: Beds and workstations

sections.text: A style is a file in `villages/`: the biomes it builds in, the well, the lamp post, the kinds of buildings with weights and maximum counts, each with one or several designs, the street plans (main street, cross, T, L, ring road, branching roads, winding or straight), the road surfaces for main roads and side roads (one chosen per village, with an optional slab for steps), the crops of the fields and the foundation block and a palette that swaps blocks of the houses. A kind can have rules: a chance per village, a smallest village size (the length of all its roads) or water within reach (then it gets a jetty). A style can stand over water on stilts, with boardwalks for roads and the swamp around it shaped into marshland with pools, mud and grass. The houses are ordinary structures; `choices` (block swaps, one option per house) and optional `parts` with a chance (chimney, flowers, shed) make every house different. A file with `extends` changes a style or makes a new one from it, and its `add` appends biomes, crops, kinds of buildings and street plans, so several mods can each add a crop to the plains. A mod can add a style for its own biome, a new style from the base game's houses with another palette, or new house designs.
sections.title: Villages in mods

sections.text: The weather is the same in the whole world. A clear spell lasts 5 to 25 minutes; then it rains for 2.5 to 10 minutes, or, with a chance of 25 in 100, a thunderstorm rages for 2 to 6 minutes; after that it clears up again. Rain and thunder come and go over 10 seconds: clouds cover the sky, it grows darker, the fog comes closer and the sky lights the land less. Each world has its own course of weather, given by its seed.
sections.title: Clear, rain and thunderstorms

sections.text: Rain and snow fall only where the sky is open: not under a roof, a tree or an overhang. In cold biomes (taiga, tundra) it snows instead of raining, and in every other biome it snows from 150 blocks up (in the mountains from their snow line). In the desert it stays dry, although the sky darkens there too. You hear the rain around you, muffled under a roof.
sections.title: Rain and snow

sections.text: In a thunderstorm lightning strikes now and then within 48 blocks of a player, on average every 10 seconds per player, only where it rains (not into snow or the desert). The flash lights up the sky at once; the thunder follows as late as sound needs for the distance: about three seconds per kilometre. A strike hurts everyone within 3 blocks by 5 health (armour takes part of it) and sets them alight; it may light a few fires where it strikes, but only while fire spreads (`fireSpread`) and within the limits of fire.
sections.title: Thunderstorms

sections.text: Rain puts out the fires it falls on, sooner or later (the older the fire, the sooner), and fire does not spread into the rain; fire on a magma block burns on. It also puts out burning players and creatures, and it keeps farmland under the open sky wet like water nearby. It never fills the world with water. Where it snows, a thin snow cover settles bit by bit on the tops of solid blocks under the open sky, not under a roof, on ice, glass or leaves, and only one layer per spot. Snow does not melt again.
sections.title: What rain and snow do

sections.text: `/weather` shows the weather. Operators set it with `/weather clear`, `/weather rain` or `/weather thunder`, for a number of seconds (`/weather rain 120`) or as long as the course of the world says. With the game rule **weatherCycle** off (`/gamerule weatherCycle false`) the weather stays as it is until it is set again; the showcase world starts that way, with a clear sky.
sections.title: Changing the weather

sections.text: A full day lasts 600 s. The world is generated from its seed while you explore it; only what you change is saved.
sections.title: Day and night

sections.text: Water and lava flow from their sources; a bucket takes a source and pours it elsewhere. Where lava meets water it hardens into obsidian or cobblestone. Lava lights its surroundings, burns items and hurts.
sections.title: Water and lava

sections.text: Ice, packed ice and blue ice are slippery. On them you speed up slowly and keep sliding when you let go, about two blocks from a walk on ice and a little farther on blue ice; your top speed stays the same. Creatures and dropped items slide too, and creatures walk round ice where the way round is short. A minecart off the rails coasts far on ice, while on other ground it stops after a short slide.
sections.title: Slippery ground

sections.text: Abandoned mine shafts lie deep underground: corridors of wooden supports on two or three levels below a central room, joined by staircases. Some corridors carry rails, and now and then a chest minecart with loot stands on them. Where a corridor crosses a cave, it runs on a plank bridge held up by pillars. Cobwebs hang in the corners, thickest around the spawners of cave spiders. Dead ends sometimes lead to a storeroom. Some mine shafts come up to the surface: look for a small wooden headframe with a ladder going down, most often in the mountains.
sections.title: Mine shafts

sections.text: Desert temples stand alone in the desert, and some desert villages are built around one. Climb down the ladder at the back of the hall into the dark cellar: four chests hold gold, emeralds and now and then diamonds, guarded by a sand golem. It attacks whoever comes within a few blocks of its cellar and returns there. A sand golem that touches a water source block crumbles into four blocks of sand and a carved sandstone head; a block without room drops as an item (with the game rule mobGriefing off the whole build drops as items). Its arms fall as sand and can fill the water they land in. While fewer golems guard the cellar than it holds (one), a new one appears in the cellar after 120 s (in a cellar seen for the first time since the world was loaded, after 60 s), as long as the cellar is dark (block light at most 7), no player is closer than 12 blocks and one is within 48 blocks. A sand farm: dig holes one block deep into the cellar floor, pour water into them, keep the cellar dark and wait a little away from it; a new golem appears on the dry floor beside the water and crumbles at once (a cellar full of water stays empty). Its arms stand beside its middle, left and right of where it looks, and fall to the floor: a hole right beside its feet fills with sand. Place the holes diagonally next to the golem's spot (it touches them, its arms miss them) or keep the falling sand off them with a block. That gives at most 120 blocks of sand and 30 heads per hour and temple. The sand fills the cellar until you dig it out.
sections.title: Desert temples and sand golems

sections.text: Jungle temples stand alone in the jungle, overgrown with moss and vines. Climb down the ladder at the back of the hall: a corridor with a stone pressure plate leads to a room with three levers on its wall. Stepping on the plate makes the dispenser beside it shoot an arrow at you. Two of the levers sit on dispensers that shoot arrows into the room; the left one opens the hidden chamber with two chests next to the room (a signal torch behind the wall holds two sticky pistons out, and the lever puts it out). Dispensers shoot arrows and other ammunition as projectiles you can pick up again.
sections.title: Jungle temples

sections.text: Witch huts stand on stilts in the swamp, often over water, with a cauldron and potted plants inside. A witch lives there: while fewer witches stay at the hut than it holds (one), a new one appears inside after 120 s, as long as the hut is dark (block light at most 7), no player is closer than 10 blocks and one is within 48 blocks. A witch throws splash potions: poison while you are not poisoned, then harming. A splash reaches everything living around the place it bursts, the weaker the further away. Hurt, she drinks a potion of healing for a moment and throws nothing meanwhile; milk takes the poison away again.
sections.title: Witch huts and witches

sections.text: Here and there the remains of an old portal stand in the open: a broken frame of obsidian and crying obsidian amid red rubble and magma, with fallen blocks around it and a chest of gold tools, gold armour, flint and obsidian beside it. Small ruins stand in many biomes, sunken ones are half buried in the ground, large ones stand in mountains, forests, taiga and tundra; no two are quite alike. The portal leads nowhere. Crying obsidian glows faintly (light 10) and, like obsidian, needs a diamond pickaxe. In plains and birch forests, and in sandstone in the desert, wells stand alone: a shaft of water sources four blocks deep under a little roof, a source of water far from any lake. Rare oases lie in the desert: a pool with sand at its bottom, grass, sugar cane and two palm-like trees.
sections.title: Ruined portals, wells and oases

sections.text: Old stone towers stand on the coasts, on low land with the open sea close by. A ladder in one corner leads up through every floor to the top room, where a chest holds gunpowder, explosives, iron, gold, food and now and then an emerald or a diamond. Beware: the stone pressure plate in front of the chest sits on explosives hidden in the floor, and stepping on it sets them off. Open the chest from the side, or break the plate first.
sections.title: Coastal towers

item:qtcraft:healing_potion.text: What a witch drinks when she is hurt: it heals her by 4. There is no brewing yet, so players cannot make or drink it.

item:qtcraft:hopper_minecart.name: qtcraft:hopper_minecart
item:qtcraft:hopper_minecart.text: A minecart that carries a Signal Hopper: it pulls items from a container above its rail and picks up items lying on its way, one item per hopper step. item:qtcraft:minecart.name: qtcraft:minecart
item:qtcraft:minecart.text: Set it down on a rail and get in with a use; sneak to get out. It rolls on along the track, faster downhill; the forward key pushes it while you ride. One hit breaks it.
item:qtcraft:minecart.title: Minecart

item:qtcraft:mushroom_stew.name: qtcraft:mushroom_stew

item:qtcraft:snowball.title: Snowball

item:qtcraft:spark_gel.text: The glowing gel of Kjuts. With a piece of coal it makes four gunpowder.

table:armour.text: Armour is worn in four slots next to the character in the inventory: drag it there, shift-click it or right-click with it in the hand. Every armour point takes 4 % off the blows of creatures and the burns of lava and magma, up to 20 points (80 %); falls and hunger go through. Each such hit wears every worn piece by a quarter of the damage (at least 1); a piece breaks when its durability is used up. Two worn pieces of the same kind in the crafting grid make one with both durabilities plus 5 %.
table:armour.title: Armour

table:blast.text: How much of an explosion's force a block soaks up before it breaks: the higher, the safer (stone 6, obsidian 1200). Blocks without a value of their own resist as much as their hardness (seconds to break by hand); unbreakable blocks never break in an explosion, and liquids soak up 100.
table:blast.title: Blast resistance

table:fuels.text: Machines such as the furnace burn one fuel item at a time while they have something to process. The times are at machine speed 1.
table:fuels.title: Fuels

table:light.text: Blocks that give light, brightest first. Light loses one level per block it travels. The creature pages tell how dark it must be for them to appear.
